rv.q: 'How to Defend Yourself' is a tumultuous and surprisingly entertaining investigation of how all of us are warped by rape culture.
Liliana Padilla's 'How to Defend Yourself' is a hilarious and unsettling play about exercises...which makes for rich material.

For as much as the play aims to engage the audience in a fly-on-the-wall view of a group of people...it still neglects to provide the necessary context to make the pre-existing relationships and the character arcs feel real.
It's an exquisite balancing act and she rarely, if ever, puts a foot wrong.
Liliana Padilla's sharply excellent play...has a visually striking denouement that gives an equivalent frisson of shock.
It should first be said that How to Defend Yourself, directed beautifully in its New York premiere by Tony winner Rachel Chavkin, is surprisingly hilarious considering its dark subject matter.
How to Defend Yourself is messy and sometimes feels less like a drama than a polemic, but people are going to be talking about it, and maybe that talk will wise some of them up.
Liliana Padilla's 'How to Defend Yourself' has its moments of strength...The scene is meticulously choreographed, but it doesn't feel like a polished performance.
Women remain uniquely vulnerable, this play reminds us, especially if they fail to heed Padilla’s advice to speak up and use their voice.
If you've already guessed this is an exercise in 21st century women's empowerment, you're on the right track.
The story zigs and zags and never lands.
